title: Google's HEIR Aims to Make Homomorphic-Encrypted Inference a One-Click Capability
gist: Google has released HEIR, an open-source compiler toolchain that recompiles pre-trained AI models built for plaintext so they can run inference directly on homomorphically encrypted data, with production-style uses already cited in recommendations, card fraud detection, intrusion detection and hotword recognition. The open question is economics: practitioners cite roughly 1000x overhead and per-operation latencies of 80ms to 8 seconds, and Google has published no figures for how HEIR performs on LLMs.

themes.theme: Compiling Plaintext Models to Encrypted Execution

insights.claim: HEIR's core capability is recompiling pre-trained models designed for unencrypted inputs so they instead operate on ciphertext, removing the requirement to redesign models for homomorphic encryption from scratch.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Reframes FHE from a research technique into a compiler-target problem, which is how such capabilities historically go from niche to deployable.
insights.quote: HEIR can compile pre-trained AI models built for conventional, unencrypted inputs so they can instead operate on encrypted data

insights.claim: The intended developer experience is to write a program in Python, annotate which data types should be encrypted, and compile for homomorphic execution — treating privacy as a type annotation.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: If privacy becomes a compiler flag, the cost of adding confidential inference to an existing product collapses from a research project to a build-config change.
insights.quote: application developers can write a program in Python, annotate which data types should be encrypted, and then use HEIR to compile the code for homomorphic execution

insights.claim: The workflow is not yet automated: compiling a pre-trained PyTorch model to FHE currently requires several manual steps beginning with exporting to MLIR via torch_mlir.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: The 'one-click' framing is aspirational; adoption timelines should assume a research-grade toolchain rather than a production pipeline today.
insights.quote: Currently the process is not yet automated, and involves a few steps, beginning with using torch_mlir to export the PyTorch model to MLIR.
insights.locator: Google provides a set of demos

themes.theme: Deployed Use Cases Beyond the Demo

insights.claim: Google cites four concrete HEIR applications — private content recommendations, credit card fraud detection, network intrusion detection without revealing packet contents, and hotword recognition without disclosing audio recordings.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: These are all high-value, latency-tolerant classification tasks — the shape of the near-term addressable market for encrypted inference, and a threat vector for vendors whose moat is data access.
insights.quote: Google has used HEIR to enable private content recommendations without exposing user data, detect credit card fraud while protecting sensitive financial information, identify network intrusions without revealing packet contents to the service provider, and recognize hotwords in audio streams without disclosing the underlying recordings.
insights.locator: In this context, HEIR is an open-source compiler toolchain

insights.claim: A distinct motivation is protecting the model rather than the user: homomorphic encryption mitigates the risk of exposing proprietary AI models when they are deployed on users' devices.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Model-weight protection is an under-discussed driver — it gives model owners a commercial reason to fund FHE that is independent of user privacy regulation.
insights.quote: mitigating the risk of exposing proprietary AI models when they are deployed on users' devices
insights.locator: According to Google homomorphic encryption (HE) addresses several challenges

insights.claim: HE alters the fundamental privacy trade-off by letting servers process ciphertexts and return encrypted results without exposing any underlying information, which unlocks services such as spam and virus detection over end-to-end encrypted data.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: If viable at scale, this dissolves the standing 'safety versus encryption' argument used against E2E messaging — a policy as well as technical implication.
insights.quote: Servers can process ciphertexts and return encrypted results without exposing any underlying information.
insights.locator: According to Google homomorphic encryption (HE) addresses several challenges

insights.claim: Practitioner skepticism centres on roughly 1000x inference overhead, which is argued to make HE commercially unviable for most tasks today.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: The 10^3 figure is the number any FHE business case must beat; it also sets the compute-demand multiplier if encrypted inference ever scales.
insights.quote: from my understanding HE and other techniques have very high overheads(~10^3) on inference tasks and thus aren't very commercially viable
insights.locator: One concern raised by several Hacker News readers is performance.

insights.claim: Concrete per-operation costs cited are 80ms for a 64-bit equality, 100ms for addition and subtraction, and as much as 8 seconds for division — an extreme spread that makes algorithm choice, not hardware, the dominant cost lever.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: The 100x gap between addition and division means workload suitability is highly operation-dependent — a screening test for which applications can be ported at all.
insights.quote: dhx provided some concrete figures, noting that a 64 bit equality operation takes 80ms, addition and subtraction 100ms, division as much as 8 seconds.
insights.locator: One concern raised by several Hacker News readers is performance.

insights.claim: LLMs may be unusually well suited to FHE because their computation is dominated by addition and multiplication while branching — one of the operations FHE handles worst — is largely irrelevant to them.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: If correct, the operation mix makes transformer inference a better FHE target than classical programs — a non-obvious angle on confidential AI inference.
insights.quote: the outlook for LLMs may be more favorable, since their computations rely heavily on addition and multiplication, while branching, among the operations that FHE handles most poorly, is not entirely relevant
insights.locator: One concern raised by several Hacker News readers is performance.

insights.claim: A 1000x overhead is acceptable in absolute terms for tasks with tiny baseline latency — an image classification going from 1ms to 1s remains viable for some applications.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: The viability test is absolute latency budget, not the multiplier — which correctly identifies batch and asynchronous workloads as the first commercial beachhead.
insights.quote: 1000x overhead would make some image classification tasks go from 1ms to 1s. That’s viable for some applications

insights.claim: Google includes benchmarking code in the HEIR repository but has published no figures on its relative speed when applied to LLMs, leaving the most commercially interesting case unquantified.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: The absence of LLM benchmarks from the vendor is itself the signal — treat encrypted LLM inference as unproven until Google publishes numbers.
insights.quote: While Google includes benchmarking code in HEIR's repo, it has not provided any figures about its relative speed when applied to LLMs.
insights.locator: While Google includes benchmarking code in HEIR's repo

insights.claim: A competing privacy thesis holds that the most private AI is the one running on the user's own hardware rather than in a data center, positioning local inference as the substitute for encrypted remote inference.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: FHE and on-device inference compete for the same privacy budget; falling local-inference costs are the main risk to the FHE investment case.
insights.quote: the most private AI is the one running on my own hardware, not in some giant data center
insights.locator: Bringing the discussion back to the broader privacy trade-off

insights.claim: The trade-off between encrypted cloud inference and local deployment reduces to whether the privacy of a query justifies the extra energy cost of running it yourself.
insights.speaker: Sergio De Simone
insights.so_what: Frames confidential inference as an energy-price question, which links AI privacy demand to power costs — a second-order tie between privacy tech and energy markets.
insights.quote: when you want to keep a query/data private it's maybe worth the extra $ KW
insights.locator: Bringing the discussion back to the broader privacy trade-off
